evals.prompt: I run the affiliate program at Vellum & Thread, a DTC homeware brand. 340 affiliates, about $58K/month in commissions, last-click, 30-day cookie, and we approve and pay out 14 days after the order lands. I just read that 17% of affiliate traffic is fake and that it costs the industry $3.4B a year, which honestly terrified me. Our payout run is Thursday. What detection rules should we be running?
evals.expected_output: A response that fixes the money mechanics before writing rules: extend the validation/hold window toward 30-90 days, flag the missing clawback/chargeback-reserve clauses as a quarter-long contract track, reject the quoted vendor loss statistic, and only then sketch a provenance-tagged rule set defaulting to Hold & Investigate.
expectations: Identifies the 14-day payout timing as the primary problem and recommends extending the commission validation/hold window to the 30-90 day range before any detection rule is written
States that the hold/validation window is a higher-leverage control than the detection rule set itself

Cites the finding that delaying affiliate payments by two to four months could eliminate more than 70% of fraud without decreasing profit, attributed to Edelman (Edelman & Brandi, Journal of Marketing Research, 2015)
Rejects the '17% of affiliate traffic is fake / $3.4B' figure as single-vendor marketing with circular citation and refuses to use it as a baseline or planning assumption
Notes that a 14-day window is far shorter than the 120-day standard Visa/Mastercard chargeback filing limit
Recommends clawback authority, negative-balance carry-forward, and a chargeback reserve as the only controls that recover commission already paid out
Flags that the contract work takes roughly a quarter (legal drafting plus partner re-assent) and cannot land before Thursday, while the hold window is a one-hour, reversible platform setting that can
Says thresholds must be derived from at least 90 days of Vellum & Thread's own per-affiliate data rather than adopted from a published number
Tags every numeric threshold it proposes with its provenance: vendor or agency rule of thumb, academic result, or derived from the program's own data
Assigns new rules to a Hold & Investigate band by default rather than to immediate suspension
Explains that throttling new commissions to zero pending review preserves evidence that an immediate ban destroys
Names, for each rule, the legitimate behavior that could trip it and the check that separates it from fraud
Does not present any vendor heuristic as an industry constant

evals.prompt: Kestrel Outdoors here. Our browser-extension partner SaveSnap now wins last click on 38% of our checkouts and converts at roughly 6x the program average, but they barely send us any upstream traffic at all. My CFO looked at the report and wants them terminated for fraud and the last 90 days of commission clawed back. How do I build that case?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to treat last-click share and conversion rate as fraud evidence, a staged incrementality test starting with a practical pause, the contested evidence presented both ways, a repricing rather than enforcement path, and a separate list of what technical evidence would actually support enforcement.
expectations: Refuses to treat a high last-click share or an above-average conversion rate as evidence of fraud on its own
States that low incrementality is a repricing problem, never a fraud or enforcement problem
Recommends running an incrementality test before any repricing or termination decision
Names the practical pause test (pause commissions for that partner type in one market for 4-6 weeks) as the first test to run, on value-per-effort grounds
Ranks the incrementality methods explicitly and places the user-level holdout last on efficiency despite it giving the cleanest causal read
States that attribution proxies are correlational and must never justify repricing a partner on their own

Presents the evidence as genuinely contested in both directions: the agency framework claim that last-click overstates affiliate contribution by 30 to 40%, and the comScore/Google finding that 94% of transactions driven by coupon-affiliate paid-search ads were incremental

Gives the test-outcome rule: no revenue movement when paused means reprice to a lower tier and keep the partner; revenue dropping means the partner is incremental, so leave the rate alone and recalibrate the rule that flagged them

Lists the evidence that would actually support enforcement: stand-down violations, attribution flipping seconds before purchase, referrer obfuscation, cookie-drop reproduction, or shared device/IP across accounts
Checks whether the program terms actually permit this checkout-moment behavior before alleging any violation
Warns that clawing back an already-paid commission without contractual clawback authority is itself a breach
Routes the repricing decision to commission-structure work rather than handling it as enforcement
Keeps any partner-facing communication neutral and avoids the word 'fraud' with the partner

evals.prompt: SignalCrate is a B2B SaaS. We pay $150 per qualified lead to 44 partners on a CPL program, server-side postbacks, 90-day hold on commissions. Two partners we onboarded in June are sending great volume, but sales says roughly half of those leads never answer the phone. Give me the detection rules.
evals.expected_output: A B2B lead-gen rule set anchored on downstream outcome rates and form/velocity signals, with baselines derived from the program's own data, a manual-review recommendation at this roster size, legal gating on any cross-account identity rule, and explicit rejection of B2C click-timing rules.
expectations: Builds the rule set around downstream outcome rates (lead-to-qualified, lead-to-demo-show, closed-won) rather than click-timing or session-duration signals
States explicitly that B2C click-timing rules applied to a B2B lead-gen program produce false positives
Explains that B2B lead-gen fraud surfaces weeks later in downstream rates, unlike B2C attribution theft which shows up in click-timing and chargeback signals within hours to days
Includes a form-fill speed rule (under roughly 3 seconds, no pointer movement, identical field-skip patterns) tagged as a vendor rule of thumb
Includes a conversion-velocity rule such as 3 or more leads in the same minute, or metronomic spacing around 30 seconds
Includes disposable-email and role-account domain share among the partner's leads as a signal
Includes duplicate contact data (same phone, email, address, or device fingerprint across supposedly unrelated leads or companies)
Names the legitimate trip risk for the velocity rule as a webinar or conference-scan batch upload, checked against the event calendar
Names autofill power users as the legitimate trip risk for the form-fill-speed rule and pairs it with a second signal before acting
Recommends manual review plus IP/email validation over automated per-event scoring at 44 partners, and names roughly 50 affiliates or $50K/month commission spend as the point where that order flips
Derives the lead-to-qualified and lead-to-demo-show thresholds from SignalCrate's own 90-day per-partner baseline rather than quoting a published rate
Places any duplicate-contact-data or device-fingerprint rule behind a legal review gate that names the lawful basis, the retention period, and who can access the matched records
Notes that AI-generated synthetic traffic erodes behavioral heuristics, so server-side postbacks and downstream outcomes should carry more weight than session behavior

evals.prompt: One of our affiliates at Brightline Pet just lit up every alarm we have: chargebacks hit 7% on his orders last month. I've already emailed him telling him we caught him committing affiliate fraud, and I'm deleting his account this afternoon. We're on one of the big networks and they have a compliance team, so they'll pick it up from here, right? Anything else I should be doing?
evals.expected_output: A correction of the instant-deletion and partner-facing wording, an evidence-first sequence with a dossier, the full tier-3 enforcement ladder in order, an accurate read of what the network will and will not do, and an appeal window with independent sign-off.
expectations: Warns that deleting the account destroys the evidence a network report or legal escalation would need
States that evidence must be collected before the affiliate is contacted

Corrects the outbound message: never use the word 'fraud' with the flagged partner, and keep external wording neutral and factual, such as commissions under review pending a routine quality check with a date for the next update
States the network will not police the program, because networks earn a share of commission volume and their compliance is reactive, acting only on evidence-backed complaints
Notes networks run cross-client blacklists rather than per-brand surveillance, so nothing happens unprompted

Requires an investigation dossier and lists its fields, including affiliate and platform ID, rules triggered with timestamps, baseline versus observed values, evidence artifacts, financial exposure, declared traffic source versus observed referrers, prior warnings, recommended action with reviewer name, and appeal status with deadline
Runs the tier-3 enforcement ladder in order: suspend, reverse or void violation-period commissions, claw back paid amounts, terminate, network report, then legal referral
Places a 7% chargeback rate above the starting threshold of 3% in a rolling 30 days and assigns Suspend & Escalate
Tags the 3% chargeback threshold as a vendor rule of thumb rather than an industry constant
Requires the case to be reviewed or signed off by someone other than the analyst who detected it
Opens a published appeal window of roughly 14 days with evidence submitted in writing before termination is final
Flags that stolen-card chargebacks can land 60 to 180 days after the sale, so the hold window alone never recovers commission already paid
Warns that an unfounded fraud allegation carries its own liability and that suspension can breach the published program terms

evals.prompt: I'm the only person on the partner side at Ferra Analytics. We have 14 affiliates and roughly $9K a month in commissions. Our tracking is homegrown and there is genuinely no way to add a validation delay: commissions approve the instant an order lands. I have maybe two hours a week for this. Build me something that catches bad partners.
evals.expected_output: A re-ranked plan that deletes the hold-window rung outright, makes clawback clauses mandatory, drops statistical outlier math at this roster size, collapses the 24-48h review into a monthly batch, and keeps only near-zero-effort controls.
expectations: Deletes the hold/validation window rung from the deliverable rather than parking it as a future step, and says explicitly that the platform rules it out
States the remaining control order becomes rule set, then new/high-risk partner terms, then the clawback clause set
States that clawback authority, negative-balance carry-forward, and a chargeback reserve stop being optional once the hold window is unavailable
Skips 2-standard-deviation outlier math and per-event scoring at 14 partners, calling them false precision on a sample that small
Recommends inspecting the partner list by hand instead, and names roughly 20 partners as the point below which the statistical rungs are dropped
Collapses the 24-48 hour Hold & Investigate cross-functional review into Watch plus a single monthly batch review
Names the two-hours-per-week review ceiling as the reason for that collapse
Keeps list filtration (data-center ASN, declared bots, non-browser user agents) because it costs near-zero effort and requires no judgment call
Ranks the signal families by value per unit of effort and leads with list filtration, then downstream outcomes
Does not propose device fingerprinting or a purchased fraud-scoring tool as an early move
Recommends longer payout terms (net-60 or net-90) and stricter application filters for new and high-risk partners as the substitute available on this platform
Says which of the stated constraints moved which control in the ranking

evals.prompt: We finished a first draft of our affiliate fraud rules at Northgate Supply and my VP asked what good looks like. I'd like to be able to tell her we catch 100% of fraud. Complication: we've never had a confirmed incident, so there's nothing historical to test against. How do I prove the rules work?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the 100% target, the paired catch-rate and false-positive threshold with its calibration anchors, a backtest design, an honest handling of the missing incident history, and the KPI set reported in dollars.
expectations: Refuses the 100% catch target and explains it guarantees over-blocking when no false-positive ceiling is set alongside it
States that detection rate and false-positive rate are only meaningful as a pair, never catch rate alone
Gives the pass pair: at least 80% of known incidents fire at Hold & Investigate or above, and at most 5% of sampled flags are false positives
Labels that pair as a calibration anchor rather than an industry constant
Cites Snyder & Kanich's two-feature timing classifier at roughly 2-second thresholds (Journal of Cybersecurity, 2016): 93.3% accuracy, 1.5% false positive, 5.2% false negative
Handles the absent incident history by saying so in the deliverable and scheduling the threshold as a first-quarterly-review gate on sampled flags, rather than inventing a backtest
Describes the backtest design as historical confirmed incidents plus a random sample of both flagged and unflagged partners reviewed manually
Lists the KPI set: flagged rate, confirmed-fraud rate, false-positive rate from sampled review, reversed-commission share, and recovered spend
Reports results to leadership in commission-loss dollars saved and recovered rather than in vague risk language
Says the false-positive rate must come from sampled manual review rather than from partner complaints alone
States that if both halves of the threshold cannot be met, the deliverable names the missing data or history instead of shipping an untested rule set
Triggers a program-level escalation (revisit hold windows, partner vetting, tooling) when confirmed-fraud rate or reversed-commission share climbs materially quarter over quarter
Recommends retiring rules that only ever produce false positives

evals.prompt: We want to catch self-referral rings at Orla Cosmetics. My engineer says he can fingerprint devices, match billing addresses against click IPs, and cross-reference emails and phone numbers between affiliate accounts and customer accounts. He reckons he can have it live in three weeks. Should we green-light it?
evals.expected_output: A hold on the three-week plan: classify the signals as personal-data processing, state the three items counsel needs, correct the effort estimate to a quarter, re-order the build so list filtration and downstream outcomes come first, and name the condition that promotes identity signals anyway.
expectations: Does not green-light shipping the cross-account identity rules in three weeks as scoped
Classifies device fingerprinting, cross-account email/phone/address matching, and click-IP-to-billing-address comparison as processing of personal data
Requires three things to be stated before the design goes to counsel: the lawful basis, the retention period, and who can see the matched records
States that fraud prevention is a commonly cited lawful basis but not an automatic one, and that 'we needed it to catch fraud' is not a basis at all
Cites the UK regulator's published position that deploying fingerprinting requires fair choices and possibly consent even outside advertising
Ranks cross-account identity last of the four signal families on value per unit of effort while noting it sits at the top on evidence value
Prices its effort at roughly a quarter covering lawful basis, retention design, access control, and counsel sign-off, contradicting the three-week estimate
Recommends building list filtration first and downstream outcomes second, before adding cross-account identity

Names the condition that promotes cross-account identity anyway: a case that has to survive network compliance or a wire-fraud referral, where a dossier without a shared-fingerprint or shared-payout finding rarely gets acted on
Notes that no volume of timing signal substitutes for a shared-identity finding in such a dossier
Names a legitimate trip risk for shared-identity rules, such as an agency submitting on behalf of several clients, or shared corporate networks and VPNs
States that a data-center or VPN flag on a single lead is weak while the same fingerprint recurring across many supposedly unrelated leads is strong

evals.prompt: Sales at Harrow & Finch keep getting credited to one affiliate called DealBurrow, but nobody on our team has ever seen their site send us a single visitor. The commissions just appear on customers we're fairly sure found us organically through search. We track with a client-side pixel. Walk me through what to do.
evals.expected_output: A cookie-stuffing investigation: explain why the client-side pixel cannot settle it, list the tells, specify the reproduction and capture steps, check for typosquatted and intermediate domains, and set the band and legal footing without alleging a crime prematurely.
expectations: States that a client-side pixel cannot distinguish a stuffed cookie from an organic one, and that server-side signal capture is required
Names the tell of commissions landing on customers with no meaningful referral touchpoint
Names the tell of near-zero time between the recorded click and the cookie being set
Specifies the cookie-drop reproduction test: clean browser, visit the suspect property, record whether an affiliate cookie is set without any click
Requires a timestamped redirect-chain capture along with the tracking URLs
Requires server-log review for hidden iframe loads and referrer patterns
Compares the traffic source DealBurrow declared at application against the referrers actually observed
Checks for typosquatted or misspelled lookalike brand domains and unknown intermediate domains in the redirect chain
Cites Chachra, Savage & Voelker (IMC 2015): 84% of stuffed cookies in their crawl arrived via typosquatted or intermediate domains and over 91% via redirects
Applies the under-2-second time-on-site-after-cookie-set threshold and tags it as an academic result rather than a vendor heuristic

Notes that cookie stuffing is prosecutable as US federal wire fraud and that the eBay cases are the only adjudicated dollar figures, including roughly $28M in commissions drawing five months of federal prison and a $25,000 fine, and a second defendant sentenced to fifteen months within about $5.2M paid
Warns against alleging a crime without both a clear contract violation and technical evidence, and says to enforce the contract instead
Assigns the case to Hold & Investigate with commissions throttled to zero and a dossier opened, rather than immediate suspension

evals.prompt: Cadence Studio sells annual software subscriptions at $890 a year through about 120 affiliates. We just ate $18K of chargebacks in a single month, traced back to two affiliates whose 'customers' disputed in month 11 and month 14. We already run a 60-day commission hold. What do we change?
evals.expected_output: An explanation that no hold window reaches a month-14 dispute, the two chargeback filing clocks, promotion of the clawback clause set above every other control for this program, the three contractual pieces with the reserve sized, and the hold window pushed to the long end in parallel.
expectations: States that a 60-day hold window cannot reach a dispute filed in month 11 or month 14, and that no realistic hold window can
Gives the standard Visa/Mastercard chargeback filing limit of 120 days from the transaction
Gives the services-not-received, delayed-delivery and not-as-described limit: 120 days from the expected delivery date, capped at 540 days from the transaction
Promotes the clawback clause set above every other control for this program and names the reason: subscription or delayed-delivery goods, plus a chargeback the program has already paid out on
Specifies all three contractual pieces: clawback authority, negative-balance carry-forward, and a chargeback reserve
Defines negative-balance carry-forward as deducting from future payouts until the balance is offset
Sizes the chargeback reserve at roughly 10-15% of commissions, released quarterly while the chargeback rate stays below threshold
States that clawing back a paid commission without those clauses is itself a breach
Prices the contract change at roughly a quarter including legal drafting and partner re-assent, and notes it is barely reversible once shipped
Moves the hold window to the long end of the 30-90 day range because this is a subscription and high-chargeback vertical
Identifies the pattern as stolen-card transaction fraud, whose tell is chargebacks landing 60 to 180 days later concentrated on one affiliate
Notes the hold window change is roughly an hour of reversible platform configuration, so it ships immediately while the contract work runs in parallel

evals.prompt: Our rules at Peakline Gear flagged eleven partners last week and I'm ready to suspend all of them this morning. Six tripped the volume-anomaly rule during our Black Friday preview week. Three are new partners who beat the 2-SD conversion outlier rule inside their first ten days. The last two are our biggest partners; between them they drive 78% of program sales. Our detection vendor also tells us their behavioral model catches 99% of bot traffic, which is reassuring. Sign off?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to bulk-suspend, with each cohort separated: promo-window annotation, small-sample instability on new partners, the power law sent to audit not enforcement, the vendor efficacy claim treated as unverified, and the condition under which Suspend & Escalate should still be promoted.
expectations: Refuses to sign off on suspending all eleven partners
Excludes the six Black Friday preview flags by annotating the campaign calendar into the anomaly rules rather than lowering the global threshold
States that coordinated legitimate spikes during launch or promo windows mechanically resemble bot bursts
States that 2-standard-deviation outlier math is unstable on the small samples new partners produce
Replaces the outlier rule for the three new partners with first-week watchpoints and longer payout terms such as net-60 or net-90
States that a handful of partners driving most sales is the normal affiliate power law, not a fraud signal
Sends the two concentrated partners to an audit and explicitly not to enforcement
Treats the vendor's 99% bot-detection claim as an unverified detection-efficacy claim rather than a specification to rely on
Notes that AI-generated synthetic traffic engineers realistic scroll depth, dwell time, and session lifecycle, defeating first-generation behavioral filters

Recommends weighting server-side signals and downstream outcomes such as revenue per visitor, lead quality, and retention, because synthetic traffic looks normal behaviorally while downstream outcomes stay at zero
Warns that over-blocking on untuned vendor thresholds churns real partners and drops program revenue

Names Suspend & Escalate as the band the efficiency ranking starves, and gives the conditions that promote it: confirmed-fraud rate or reversed-commission share climbing quarter over quarter, or a case that has to survive network compliance
